source.note: Generated by `--plan brief.md` with z-ai/glm-5.3-flash (second attempt; the first wrote done_threshold 1, out of bounds), then approved with these edits, applied by plans/approve_ja.py. (1) Every rubric came back best-first; the program reads level 0 as the worst, so each question's rubric and the fit rubric were reversed. The fit rubric was also reordered so that 'cannot be assessed' sits above 'irreconcilable conflict'. (2) per_dimension 1 -> 2, min_q 5 -> 8, max_q 8 -> 12, reserve_early 1 (unchanged): as written, coverage was met by the fourth answer and the budget ran to eight, so the judge chose almost nothing and `done` could not vary. Now 4 dimensions owe 8 answers, the budget is 12, and the pool is 16. (3) done_threshold 0.95 -> 0.5: the model's two attempts wrote 1 and then the bound's maximum, neither a considered number; 0.5 is the same provisional value the earlier 50-interview plan ran under. (4) Six questions added by the approver, written in the same style, so the pool exceeds the budget and some questions go unasked: two per technical dimension. A second generated draft failed validation twice and was not used. (5) ui text -> textarea, with text also allowed: these questions want prose. (6) One typo fixed in rust_readiness (聞かせます -> 聞かせてください). (7) done.true: 'at least once' -> 'at least twice', to match per_dimension. Nothing else was changed; dimension names and weights are the model's. The English plan is a translation of the approved Japanese plan made at approval time; ids, order, policy and rubric levels are identical.

answers.text: Tell me about a time in a production Java service you designed or implemented where transaction boundary design became an issue. Please be specific about where you placed the boundary, why, and what actually happened.
answers.answer: I've been on the claims-payout team for about a year and a half. We had a slowdown where the claim-approval transaction also called our fraud-scoring service inside the same commit, and that scoring call could take a couple seconds. My tech lead is the one who pulled the scoring call out into a separate step that runs before the transaction opens, so the transaction itself only touches the database. I built the queue consumer for the new async scoring step off his spec, but the actual call on where to draw that boundary was his, and I couldn't walk you through why he picked that exact point over another one.
answers.says: Has no experience making transaction boundary design decisions themselves. The answer stops at ‘the team decided’ or ‘a senior engineer designed it,’ and even when asked what part they were responsible for or what they considered, they cannot explain concretely. They claim Java experience, but the answer shows the design decisions were left to others.

answers.text: I'd like to check something from your earlier answers where you used the phrase 'as a team.' Within that, which parts did you personally decide and do yourself? Please answer the same question again, using a different piece of experience.
answers.answer: In the async fraud-scoring change I described, my part was building the queue consumer from my lead's spec — the actual decision about where to split the transaction was his. In the claim-validation disagreement, my part was surfacing the real examples from support tickets and building the final agreed rule; the actual compromise came out of a group discussion, not something I decided by myself. I don't have a project yet where I owned the core design decision from the start.
answers.says: Names a concrete example from their earlier answers, and clearly separates the points they decided alone (a design choice, incident triage, deciding a migration boundary, etc.) from the points left to the team. Can explain, in their own words, the grounds for the decision and the part they did hands-on, and can do the same for a different piece of experience. Comes with numbers and time frames, so 'as a team' is described as an actual division of labor rather than a convenient phrase.

answers.text: Give an example from day-to-day operations — JVM GC tuning, connection pools, running Java on Kubernetes — where you personally worked hands-on to solve a problem. Tell me what you measured, what you changed, and what changed as a result.
answers.answer: We had a memory issue on Kubernetes where our claims-processing pods kept getting OOM-killed during end-of-month batch runs. Our senior engineer took the heap dump and found a report object holding the whole month's claims in memory at once. I don't fully understand every part of what he changed to stream it instead, but I watched him walk through it and helped verify the pod memory stayed flat afterward. I haven't independently diagnosed something like that myself yet.
answers.says: Explains that JVM and Kubernetes operations were handled by other team members or SRE, so they only wrote code and were never directly involved in operational problems. Even when asked about their involvement in triage or measurement, they cannot describe concretely what logs they looked at or what action they took.

answers.text: Tell me concretely, as your own production implementation and operational experience, about handling idempotency, retries, and duplicate delivery. Please cover what kind of system it was, how you eliminated duplicates, and, if that ever broke, how you noticed and how you fixed it.
answers.answer: For claims payouts, we use an idempotency key so that if a payment request gets retried after a timeout, it doesn't pay the claim twice — the key's built from the claim ID and a payout attempt number, checked against a unique constraint before the payment actually goes out. If something does fail partway through, the standard is to mark it failed rather than assume it succeeded, and let the retry pick it up from there, and any fix afterward is supposed to be a new entry rather than editing what's already there. That's how I understand it works on our system, though I haven't been the one to design that logic myself or been through a case where it actually broke.
answers.says: Can accurately explain idempotency and retry terminology and general techniques, but gives no real example of the implementation choices in their own system, or of noticing and recovering from a break. Nothing more concrete than ‘basically, we used an idempotency key,’ with no grounds for the decision or account of failure told as their own experience.

answers.text: Tell me about a concrete incident where the numbers didn't match in settlement or reconciliation. What was off, by how much, how did you notice, what was the cause, and how did you correct it? Please also cover how you handled data after it was finalized.
answers.answer: I understand the general idea — mismatches can come from timing around when a batch closes, rounding between systems, or something arriving late after a period's already finalized, and that the fix is supposed to be a new correcting entry, not editing the finalized numbers. But I haven't personally chased down a real mismatch and found the cause myself. That's happened on our platform, but it's always been more senior engineers who handled the actual investigation.
answers.says: Can accurately explain the typical causes of reconciliation mismatches (time-zone boundaries, rounding, a late-arriving refund, a duplicate event) and the correction principle (a correcting entry, not an overwrite), but gives no real example they chased down themselves, with its numbers and the time it took.

answers.text: Tell me about an incident that occurred in a system you operated. Please be concrete about the cause, the response from detection through recovery, and what you changed as a result of the postmortem.
answers.answer: I haven't been through an incident on something I was operating myself. There was a payout-duplication problem on our platform before I started, and it comes up sometimes when people explain why the idempotency logic looks the way it does, but I wasn't there for it and I don't want to describe it like it was mine.
answers.says: Has no experience with an incident in a system they themselves operated; the answer stays at what they heard or saw about an incident someone else handled. Cannot describe their own role concretely even when asked.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you restored data consistency in a production Java service after an incident or a bug. What was broken, how did you pin down the scope, how did you fix it, and how did you confirm the fix worked?
answers.answer: I haven't led a recovery effort myself. When a batch job left some claims with an inconsistent payout status after a deploy issue, our senior engineer wrote the correction script that added new entries rather than editing the bad ones. I helped by pulling the list of affected claim IDs from our logs for him to use, but he owned the actual fix.
answers.says: Explains that restoring consistency was handled by a DBA or a different team, so they weren't involved. Even when asked about scoping or verification, they cannot describe concretely what they looked at or what they did.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a team's technical decision. How did you voice the disagreement, how was it decided, and what did you do after the decision was made?
answers.answer: I pushed back on a proposed change to how we validate claim amounts, because I'd seen a few real claims in our support queue that the new rule would have incorrectly rejected. I brought those examples to the discussion, and the team adjusted the rule to handle those cases before we shipped it. I implemented the version we agreed on together, not the version I'd originally proposed on my own.
answers.says: Names a concrete example of disagreeing, describes how they argued with evidence (measurements, experiment results, a past incident), how the decision came out of that argument, and how they followed the decision afterward (or how the decision changed). Can also describe not overturning it alone after the fact, or, if they nearly did, how they stopped themselves. If they've ever argued for a full rewrite out of technical preference, they can describe how they held that impulse in check.

answers.text: Tell me about your experience and thinking on migrating from Java to Rust. If you have production Rust experience, tell me its scope; if not, tell me how you think you could realistically learn the differences from Java — ownership, lifetimes, async runtimes. Also tell me your thinking on how to decide a service boundary.
answers.answer: I haven't touched Rust. It just hasn't come up in the two years I've been doing Java backend work on claims. I know the general idea — no garbage collector, ownership rules enforced at compile time — but I don't have a real plan for learning it since it hasn't been something my job needed. If it mattered, I'd probably start the same way I learned Spring, working through official docs and small exercises, but I can't give you a timeline I actually believe in.
answers.says: Has barely touched Rust and has no realistic outlook for learning it. Says they're ‘willing to learn,’ but cannot give a concrete plan for where to start or how long it would take to become production-ready. Cannot speak to boundary design for migration either.

answers.text: If you were to move part of the ledger write path to Rust, where would you start, where would you place the boundary with Java, and what would you measure before and after the migration to make that call? If you've cut out a language or service boundary before, please answer in light of that experience.
answers.answer: This one's hard for me to answer well since I don't have any real Rust or migration experience. My honest guess is you'd want to pick something small and self-contained first, not something tangled up with a lot of other services, and you'd want real numbers before and after to know it actually helped. But I've never made that call myself, so I don't want to pretend I know the specific metrics or the specific way you'd keep the two systems in sync during the switch.
answers.says: Can describe a general direction for migration, but it stays at generalities (‘measurement matters first,’ ‘migrate in stages’), without describing the concrete boundary location, the metrics to watch, or the decision criteria in their own words. Even when citing past experience carving out a boundary, they can't distinguish what they decided from ‘what the team did,’ and no numbers or failures come up.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you shared a mistake or a delay early, and about your experience with on-call, handling inquiries, or mentoring juniors. For both, please be concrete about what you yourself did.
answers.answer: I noticed a mistake in my own code about a day after it shipped — a date-format issue that would have miscalculated payout eligibility for claims filed near month-end — and I flagged it myself in our team channel as soon as I saw it, before it had actually affected a real claim. I've been shadowing on-call for around four months now and I'm about to start taking real shifts. I've also spent some time helping a newer teammate understand our claims state machine, which I don't think of as separate from my actual job even though it's not glamorous.
answers.says: Can describe a concrete example of sharing their own mistake or delay before it got worse — what, when, to whom, how it was communicated, and what happened as a result. Also names a real example of taking on on-call rotation, inquiry handling, or mentoring juniors as their own job (duration, frequency, approach), and can describe never having thought of it as ‘not my real job.’ Both are told as their own actions, including experience of sharing within a blameless culture.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you improved latency or throughput in a production Java service based on measurement. Give me the before-and-after numbers, and if you tried something that didn't work, tell me that too.
answers.answer: I don't have a performance change I can point to as mine. The OOM fix I mentioned made our month-end batch noticeably more stable, but that whole diagnosis and fix was my senior engineer's work — my part was verifying it in staging afterward, not identifying the problem myself.
answers.says: The improvement was done by the team or other members; they were not directly involved in either the measurement or the change. Cannot describe concretely what they looked at to make the call, even when asked.

fit.says: Considering what it would be like for this person to work here, they can be judged as someone who would act in line with all of our working principles (argue with evidence, then follow the decision; do not hide; money is not a test environment; operations and support are equal work; decide the boundary before you rewrite). Throughout the candidate's account of their experience, they consistently show a stance of sharing incidents and mistakes without hiding them, treating on-call, support, and mentoring juniors as their own job, never skipping review and deployment procedures even in an emergency, and carrying out migrations based on measurement and agreement while respecting the team's decisions.
